extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent applicants/attorneys evaluating U.S. patent subject-matter eligibility (Section 101)
extracted.subtask_description: Applying the USPTO/MPEP 2106 framework to analyze whether patent claims are eligible subject matter under 35 U.S.C. §101, including the Step 1 / Step 2A (two prongs) / Step 2B analysis and related considerations (e.g., abstract-idea groupings, improvements to technology, particular treatment).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim interpretation — broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the broadest reasonable interpretation, the terms of the claim are presumed to have their plain meaning consistent with the specification as it would be interpreted by one of ordinary skill in the art. See Manual of Patent Examining Procedure (MPEP) 2111.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret claim terms in light of the specification and the ordinary artisan's understanding; do not ignore limitations; dependent claim wherein-clauses may have patentable weight. Use BRI when construing the claim for the Section 101 analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 1 — statutory category check
rubrics_metrics.description: This part of the eligibility analysis evaluates whether the claim falls within any statutory category. See MPEP 2106.03.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine whether the claim is a process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter; if not in a statutory category, stop (Step 1: NO). If yes, proceed to Step 2A.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A Prong One — does the claim recite a judicial exception?
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether the claim 'recites' a judicial exception (i.e., the judicial exception is 'set forth' or 'described' in the claim). See MPEP 2106.04.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify specific claim limitations that align with judicial exceptions (abstract ideas, laws of nature, products of nature). A limitation recites an exception if it sets forth the exception itself; use the plain meaning in light of the specification to make this determination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial exceptions — recognized groupings
rubrics_metrics.description: Judicial exceptions include: Abstract Idea: Mathematical Concept; Abstract Idea: Mental Process; Abstract Idea: Certain Methods of Organizing Human Activity; Law of Nature; Product of Nature; Multiple exceptions in same claim; No recited exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map claimed subject matter to one or more of these groupings (e.g., mathematical calculations → mathematical concept; observation/evaluation → mental process). It is sufficient to identify at least one matching exception for further analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of multiple exceptions (avoid over-parsing)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Unless it is clear that a claim recites distinct exceptions, such as a law of nature and an abstract idea, care should be taken not to parse the claim into multiple exceptions, particularly in claims involving abstract ideas." MPEP 2106.04, subsection II.B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If possible, consider limitations together as a single abstract idea rather than separately; when different abstract-idea groupings appear (e.g., mathematical concept + mental process), an examiner may treat them together for Step 2A analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A Prong Two — integration into a practical application
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether the claim as a whole integrates the recited judicial exception into a practical application of the exception (i.e., whether the claim is 'directed to' the judicial exception). This is performed by (1) identifying additional elements beyond the exception, and (2) evaluating those additional elements individually and in combination to determine whether the claim integrates the exception into a practical application. See MPEP 2106.04(d).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for additional elements that meaningfully limit the abstract idea (not merely data gathering, output, or generic computer use). Evaluate whether the claim improves the functioning of a computer/other technology, recites a particular machine/transformation, or provides other meaningful limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvement to functioning of a computer or other technology
rubrics_metrics.description: One way to determine integration into a practical application is when the claimed invention improves the functioning of a computer or improves another technology or technical field. See MPEP 2106.04(d)(1) and 2106.05(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The specification must set forth an improvement in technology and the claim itself must reflect the disclosed improvement. If both are present, this supports a finding that the claim is not directed to a judicial exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Particular treatment or prophylaxis (Prong Two consideration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Particular treatment or prophylaxis is a Prong Two consideration for medical/biotech claims: a claim that applies an abstract idea by identifying a specific patient population and administering a particular treatment may meaningfully limit the abstract idea. See MPEP 2106.04(d)(2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine whether the claim requires a particular treatment tied to a specific patient population or disease such that the abstract idea is meaningfully limited (e.g., administering Compound X to high-risk patients). Mere generic 'administer an appropriate treatment' is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Particular machine or particular transformation
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that recite a particular machine or a particular transformation can integrate an exception into a practical application (traditional 'machine-or-transformation' considerations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the claim's recited machine/transform is a meaningful, specific implementation rather than a generic invocation of a computer or routine transformation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other meaningful limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Other meaningful limitations are additional elements beyond the judicial exception that impose specific, non-generic constraints on the claimed invention and thus can integrate the exception into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for limitations that impose specific structure, steps, or technical detail that confine how the abstract idea is applied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere instructions to apply an exception (MPEP 2106.05(f))
rubrics_metrics.description: MPEP 2106.05(f) provides considerations for determining whether a claim simply recites a judicial exception with the words 'apply it' (or equivalent), i.e., mere instructions to implement an abstract idea on a computer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider (1) whether the claim recites only the idea of a solution or outcome (no details of how the solution is accomplished); (2) whether the claim invokes computers or other machinery merely as a tool to perform an existing process; and (3) the particularity or generality of the application of the judicial exception. If these point to 'apply it' language, the additional elements likely do not integrate the exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insignificant extra-solution activity (MPEP 2106.05(g))
rubrics_metrics.description: Limitations that amount to mere data gathering, insignificant extra-solution activity, or generic input/output described at a high level do not meaningfully limit an abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include 'receiving data at a computer' or 'outputting results' recited at a high level of generality. Treat such elements as insufficient to integrate an exception in Prong Two, but re-evaluate conventionality in Step 2B.

rubrics_metrics.name: Field of use / technological environment (MPEP 2106.05(h))
rubrics_metrics.description: Simply confining an abstract idea to a particular technological field or environment (e.g., 'using a neural network' or 'in network traffic') generally does not add an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A mere statement of field of use or linking to a technical environment is typically insufficient to render a claim eligible unless combined with other meaningful limitations or technical improvements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2B — inventive concept / 'significantly more' analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: This part of the eligibility analysis evaluates whether the claim as a whole amounts to significantly more than the recited exception, i.e., whether any additional elements, or combination thereof, add an inventive concept to the claim. See MPEP 2106.05.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if Prong Two fails (claim directed to an exception), examine whether unconventional, non-routine additional elements (alone or in combination) provide 'significantly more.' If not, claim remains ineligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Well-understood, routine, conventional (WURC) activity — Step 2B consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: At Step 2B, previously-identified extra-solution activities should be re-evaluated to determine whether they are well-understood, routine, and conventional in the field (MPEP 2106.05(g)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the additional elements are WURC, they cannot provide an inventive concept. If the claim elements reflect improvements beyond WURC activity, they may supply an inventive concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of mental processes and mathematical calculations as abstract ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Mental steps (observation, evaluation, judgment, opinion) and mathematical calculations (e.g., rounding, weighting, backpropagation/gradient descent) are commonly classified as abstract ideas under MPEP 2106.04(a)(2) groupings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When claim steps can be practically performed in the human mind or are mathematical concepts, treat those limitations as abstract ideas and proceed with Step 2A/2B analysis accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conventional data-gathering or lab techniques are routine
rubrics_metrics.description: Routine collection/genotyping/measurement steps recited at a high level are likely conventional (e.g., genotyping by conventional methods) and thus insufficient to provide an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify whether the specification discloses any non-routine technical implementation of data-gathering steps; absent that, treat these as WURC in Step 2B.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessing claimed remedial or real-time actions as technical improvements
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim recitations of automatic remedial actions (e.g., detecting source address in real time, dropping malicious packets, blocking future traffic) can reflect a technical improvement and may integrate an abstract idea into a practical application if the claim and specification show the improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the claimed real-time/remedial steps are specific, technical solutions that improve a technological field (e.g., network security) rather than generic results or field-of-use framing.
